title: The Price of Being Beautiful
paragraphs: Ten years ago, San Isidro was a village in the Peruvian highlands that most travellers drove past on their way to somewhere better known. Today, on a clear Saturday, its single square contains more cameras than residents. A guesthouse stands where the baker once lived, a cafe sells oat-milk coffee for twelve soles, and the old irrigation channel, along which children once raced paper boats, has been covered to make room for a terrace. By any conventional measure, the village is a success.

We should begin by acknowledging what tourism has brought. Wages have risen, a clinic has opened and young people who would once have left for Lima now find reasons to stay. Nobody in San Isidro, so far as we can tell, wishes to return to the days when a bad harvest could empty a household of its savings in a month. Those who preach nostalgia to a community that has just discovered a steady income should do so with great delicacy, and preferably from a distance.

But a success that cannot be sustained is only a delay. The village's water, which for centuries served a few hundred people, now serves several thousand visitors a month, and in the dry season the taps run for only two hours a day. Rents have risen faster than wages, and the families who made the place attractive are being quietly pushed to the margins of the settlement. When the last grandmother who sells textiles can no longer afford to live in the village, what exactly will visitors have come to see?

This is the paradox at the heart of the matter: tourism feeds on authenticity and gradually consumes it. The traveller wants a place that has not been spoiled, and the very act of arriving spoils it a little. No individual visitor is to blame, any more than a single raindrop is to blame for a flood. The responsibility lies instead with the rules, or the absence of them, that govern how the pleasure of many is allowed to turn into the burden of a few.

The remedies are neither mysterious nor cheap. A cap on daily visitors, enforced fairly, would protect the water and the peace. A tax on overnight stays, paid into a community fund, could finance housing for residents and repairs to the channel. Local ownership of the guesthouses, rather than outside investors, would keep much of the income where it is earned. Several mountain communities elsewhere have adopted such measures and have not, as was feared, been abandoned by tourists.

Some will complain that such limits are paternalistic, and that a village should be free to take every sol that comes its way. The objection deserves a hearing, but it assumes that the choice is being made by the village. In practice, decisions are often taken by regional authorities, investors and agencies, with the residents consulted afterwards, if at all. A genuine freedom to choose requires information, time and a seat at the table, none of which San Isidro has been offered.

We therefore call on the regional government to open a public consultation before approving any further hotels, and to publish the results. The aim is not to freeze the village in a picture postcard, which would be its own kind of cruelty, but to allow it to decide what it wishes to become. A place is more than its view. If we forget that, the visitors will still arrive, but they will be photographing the outside of an empty shop.

title: The Cartographer's Apprentice
focus: Past perfect, narrative reflection and subtext
paragraphs: Wanjiru had been apprenticed to the mapmaker for two years before she was allowed to draw a river. Until then, her duties had been to sharpen the pens, to mix the inks and to listen. Mr Otieno, who ran a small survey office above a tailor's shop in Nairobi, spoke while he worked, usually about the failings of other mapmakers, and she had learned to nod at the right moments. She earned twelve thousand shillings a month, which was less than her cousin made selling phone credit, and she would not have changed places for the world.

The river was a minor one, a tributary in the west that the county wished to include in a new planning map. Wanjiru traced it from the survey notes, bend by bend, and took three days over it. When she finished, Mr Otieno examined her work for a long time, saying nothing. Then he took out a magnifying glass, bent over the paper and, with a faint sigh, pointed to a single curve. 'Here,' he said. 'It is wrong. Not much. A few metres.'

She had checked it against the notes four times. When she said so, he nodded as though this were exactly the problem. 'The notes are wrong,' he said. 'The surveyor was in a hurry, I think, or in love. I have seen the river, and it does not do this.' He told her that it would be easy to leave the line as it was, because the notes were official and nobody would ever walk that bank with a ruler. Then he asked her what she wished to do.

Wanjiru did not answer at once. She thought of the three days, of the sore wrist and of the fact that to change the line would mean to begin the page again. She thought, too, of the people who would use the map: the engineers, the farmers, perhaps a family hoping to build a house near the water. A few metres, she told herself, could be nothing. A few metres could also be a front door in the river.

'I will redraw it,' she said, and her voice came out smaller than she had intended. Mr Otieno gave no sign of approval. He handed her a clean sheet and returned to his own table, where, she noticed, he did not touch his pen for a long time. It was only years later, when she had her own office and her own apprentices, that she understood that he had been watching the door, in case she changed her mind.

The new map took a week. When it was finished, it was not better to look at than the first, and nobody thanked her for it. The county, in fact, sent a short letter complaining that the delivery was late. But in March, when the heavy rains came and the tributary rose by more than a metre, the village of Kapsabet escaped, as it happened, with only a few wet floors, since a new road, planned from her map, had been placed a little farther from the bank.

Wanjiru often tells the story to her own apprentices, sometimes with the details altered, because it is a story that does not require anyone to be a hero. She tells them what Mr Otieno said when she asked, at last, why he had not simply corrected the line himself. 'A map is a promise,' he said. 'I did not want to make it for you. I wanted you to know what it felt like to keep one.'

questions.explain_es: Fue Mr Otieno quien detectó la curva incorrecta con una lupa; ella había comprobado las notas cuatro veces y coincidían.

questions.explain_es: Inferencia: años después ella entiende 'that he had been watching the door, in case she changed her mind'.

questions.explain_es: Tono: su frase 'A map is a promise' es serena y pedagógica, no amarga ni jactanciosa.

options: To suggest that Mr Otieno was joking
To describe the colour of the houses nearby

questions.explain_es: Propósito: ilustra que un error pequeño puede poner una vivienda en peligro; es la razón del dilema de Wanjiru.

options: forbid

title: To the New Nurses
paragraphs: Graduates, families, colleagues of the faculty: it is an honour to speak to you on a day on which you have every right to feel proud and, I suspect, very tired. I was a nurse for twenty-six years before I became a teacher, and the one thing I can promise you about your profession is that it will ask more of you than you expect and thank you less than you deserve. I say this not to discourage you but to prepare you, which is, after all, the whole purpose of a school.

The first thing you will learn is that care is not a feeling. It is a practice, and like every practice it is built from small, repeated actions: the hand washed again, the dose checked a third time, the call light answered at the moment when you would rather have sat down. Many people will tell you that the job requires compassion. They are right. But compassion that evaporates after a double shift is no use to anyone, and what patients need is the kind that has become a habit.

The second thing is that you will see people at their most frightened. You will see a man in his forties learn that he cannot walk, a mother who has not slept in four days and a very old woman who, at three in the morning, asks you in perfect lucidity whether she is dying. There will be no script. You will learn, as we all have, that the best answer is often not an answer. It is to stay, to sit down and to be, for a few minutes, wholly unhurried.

The third is more uncomfortable. You are entering a system that frequently asks you to do too much with too little. There will be understaffed wards, broken equipment and managers who speak of efficiency when they mean saving. In those conditions, you will be tempted to cut corners, and I will not insult you by pretending that you will never do so. What I ask is that you never stop noticing when you have. The day you no longer notice is the day that harm, which has been waiting patiently, finally enters.

Protect yourselves. I say this as plainly as I can, because it is the advice that nurses are least likely to take. You cannot pour from an empty vessel, and professional sacrifice is not a virtue when it turns into collapse. Take your breaks. Speak up when the numbers are unsafe. Find a colleague you trust and tell her the truth about your day. There is no heroism in silent suffering, and the patients you will serve tomorrow need you to be well today.

Remember also that you are not alone. Behind each one of you today stand parents who paid for your shoes and grandmothers who prayed in several languages, and ahead of you stand tens of thousands of colleagues who have done this work before and who will, on your worst night, make you a cup of tea without being asked. Nursing, whatever else it is, is a community. You are now members of it, and you will be, for the rest of your lives.

So go. Go into the clinics and the wards and the villages where you are needed. Be skilled, be steady, be kind, and be willing to be corrected. Be, when no one is watching, exactly the person you will be when everyone is. And when, in some difficult year, you wonder why you chose this, remember this room, these faces and the particular silence of a night shift in which a hand you are holding relaxes. That is the answer. It has always been the answer.
glossary: hacer las cosas a medias, ahorrarse pasos

title: Ministry Announces Official Approximate Time
focus: Passive reporting structures and mock-official language
paragraphs: MEXICO CITY. The Ministry of Punctuality yesterday unveiled a historic reform, under which all appointments in the capital will henceforth be described as 'approximately at' the time stated. Officials said the measure reflected 'the daily reality of the citizen', and noted that, in a recent survey, ninety-four per cent of respondents had not arrived anywhere on time since the previous administration. The remaining six per cent were reportedly asked to leave.

The reform, which was prepared over fourteen months by a committee of twenty-two experts, introduces three new categories of lateness. 'Slight delay' covers up to forty minutes and requires no explanation. 'Substantial delay', which runs to two hours, may be justified by pointing vaguely in the direction of the traffic. 'Delay of the third kind', lasting more than two hours, will be recognised as a natural phenomenon and will be dealt with by the Ministry of Environment.

Minister Rodrigo Valdés, who arrived at the press conference ninety minutes after its announced start, defended the policy with some emotion. 'For decades, this country has lived in a state of hypocrisy,' he said. 'Everybody pretends to be punctual, and everybody lies about it, in the lift, on the phone and in the voice messages that begin with the words, I am five minutes away. We are simply telling the truth, and we have printed it on a certificate.'

The certificate, which will be issued free of charge to every citizen at a cost of four hundred pesos, entitles the bearer to be late without remorse for a period of one year. It may be renewed on payment of a smaller fee, provided that the applicant presents proof of having waited in a queue for no fewer than three hours, a requirement the Ministry describes as 'the one point where we remain firm'.

Not everyone has welcomed the news. A spokeswoman for the national railway said that the new approximate schedules were 'broadly consistent with current practice', adding that trains would continue to depart 'when the spirit of the occasion moves them'. A group of dentists, meanwhile, expressed concern that patients might now arrive at any time during the week, a development one described as 'both hopeful and alarming'.

Economists have been quick to measure the effects. Professor Ana Beltrán, of a private university, calculated that the reform would save the country the equivalent of eleven million hours of mild resentment each year, though she acknowledged that the figure was 'a very rough guess, delivered at roughly the time the Ministry would have wanted'. She also noted that, since no one would be late any more, no one could be early, which she called 'a small loss for the already very anxious'.

At press time, the Ministry had begun work on a second package of measures, including an official calendar in which Mondays would be 'optional', and a national scale of excuses ranging from 'the bus' to 'something came up in the family'. Minister Valdés confirmed that the proposal would be debated in Congress 'at some point soon', and added that his team was confident of success 'by the end of the year, or thereabouts'.

questions.explain_es: Llegó 'ninety minutes after its announced start', lo que es parte de la ironía.

title: Memory Is Not a Recording
paragraphs: Most of us imagine memory as a kind of archive. An event happens, it is stored somewhere in the brain and, when we need it, we retrieve it more or less as it was, perhaps a little faded. The metaphor is comforting, and it is wrong. Decades of research suggest that remembering is closer to reconstruction than to playback: each time we recall an event, we assemble it afresh from fragments, expectation and whatever information has reached us since.

One of the best-known demonstrations came in 1974, when the psychologists Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer showed participants films of car accidents. Afterwards, they asked how fast the cars had been going when they 'smashed into' each other. Other participants were asked the same question, but with the verb 'hit'. Those who read 'smashed' gave noticeably higher estimates of speed. A single word, it seemed, had altered the memory of the event.

The researchers went a step further. A week later, they asked the participants whether they had seen any broken glass in the film. There had been none. Yet those who had been given the word 'smashed' were more likely to say that they had. The memory had not merely been coloured by the language; it appeared to have incorporated a detail that never existed. This is a result that has since been discussed, and sometimes over-interpreted, in countless textbooks.

The implications for the justice system are considerable. Eyewitness testimony is persuasive to juries precisely because witnesses are usually sincere. But sincerity and accuracy are different things, and a person who is entirely confident in her recollection may still be mistaken. Leading questions, repeated interviews and exposure to media coverage can all shape what a witness believes she saw. Reforms in several countries, such as recording a witness's confidence immediately after an identification, reflect this understanding.

It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that memory is hopelessly unreliable. The gist of our experiences, who was there, roughly what happened and why it mattered, tends to be remembered well. It is the details, particularly under stress and after delay, that are vulnerable. Researchers also stress that the original studies were laboratory experiments, in which participants had no personal stake in the events. Real memories of significant events may behave differently, though how differently remains a matter of ongoing study.

There is, finally, a philosophical dimension. If remembering is an act of reconstruction, then the past we carry with us is partly a creation of the present. Our memories are rewritten each time we use them, in the light of what we have since learned and what we now feel. This may sound unsettling, yet it has a benefit: it allows us to revise old injuries, to reinterpret failure and to see a difficult year with some generosity.

The practical advice is modest. Be sceptical of vivid memories that others cannot confirm, especially if they were recalled under pressure. Write down important events soon after they occur. And when somebody remembers a shared episode differently from you, resist the temptation to assume that one of you must be lying. Both of you may be telling the truth as your brain has composed it, which is rarely the same as telling the truth as it was.
glossary: interés personal, algo que está en juego

title: On Being a Guest
paragraphs: The first time I stayed in a stranger's home abroad, I was twenty-two and a student in Istanbul. My host, a retired teacher named Selma, put a glass of tea into my hand before I had put down my bag. By the time I had finished it, a second glass had appeared, and a plate of pastries, and a series of questions about my family so detailed that I began to feel I was being interviewed for a position. It was only later that I understood the whole performance as a form of welcome.

What struck me, over the following weeks, was how much of the guest's role consists of knowing how to receive. We tend to think of hospitality as an act of the host, a kind of generosity that flows in one direction. But a gift that is not accepted is hardly a gift. To refuse a third glass of tea can be understood, in some places, as a small insult, and to accept it graciously is a kind of contribution. The guest, in other words, gives something by taking.

This reciprocity is subtle and varies from one culture to the next. In some societies, it is polite to bring a present and to leave a little food on the plate; in others, the plate should be emptied, and the present opened immediately. Anyone who travels will make mistakes, and I made many. I praised a vase so enthusiastically that Selma tried to give it to me, which in her tradition was a rule and in mine an embarrassment. I took the vase, and I still have it.

Yet beneath the variations, I think there is a common structure. To be a guest is to accept a temporary condition of dependency, and this is harder than it seems. Adults who are accustomed to managing their own lives find it uncomfortable to be fed, housed and advised by someone else. We try to pay at once, to help in the kitchen, to repay the debt before it grows. A wise host often prevents this, because they understand that the debt is the point.

There is an instructive contrast with the modern idea of the hotel, or of the home rented through an application, where hospitality has become a transaction and the relationship ends at the moment of payment. I do not wish to disparage these arrangements, which are efficient and, for many people, a relief. But they offer comfort without obligation, and obligation, however inconvenient, is one of the ways in which human beings recognise one another. We remember our hosts precisely because we owe them.

It follows that the best guests are those who are willing to be a little foolish. They eat what they do not recognise, they sit through three hours of a family argument conducted in a language they barely understand, and they admit it when they have done something wrong. They show, in short, that they trust the people around them. It is a rare form of compliment, and I have seen it open doors that no amount of money could have unlocked.

I never saw Selma again after that summer, though we exchanged cards for several years. When she died, her daughter wrote to tell me, and added that my vase, or rather its twin, was still in the house. I read that line standing in a station, in the middle of a crowd, and found myself unable to move. A guest, I realised, leaves something behind in the home he visits, and the home keeps it, long after he has forgotten how to say thank you in the language that mattered.

title: Review: The Weight of Water, an Exhibition That Floods Its Own Rooms
paragraphs: Water is a gift to the curator. It can be a symbol of life, of memory, of loss, of migration, of climate, of the unconscious; it can be, as the catalogue notes of The Weight of Water insist, 'all of these simultaneously'. The new exhibition at a museum in Medellín, which gathers some forty works by artists from eleven countries, takes advantage of this generosity so energetically that by the third room one begins to feel that the water has risen above the visitor's knees.

The best works are those that resist the theme. A small video by the Brazilian artist Tatiana Moura, in which a woman washes a single plate for eleven minutes, says more about time, domestic labour and boredom than any of the surrounding installations. It never mentions water as a concept, only as a material, and it is all the better for it. Similarly, a series of photographs of Andean wells, taken without commentary, accomplishes something that the catalogue's three essays on 'liquid identity' do not.

Elsewhere, the curators have been less restrained. A large sculpture of suspended glass bottles, titled Thirst, is accompanied by a wall text of two hundred words explaining that thirst is both literal and metaphorical. This is the sort of information that visitors can supply for themselves, and which they may resent being told. The text, which refers to the work as 'an invitation to dialogue', reminded me that art, like water, is most useful when it is not announced.

There is, to be fair, a serious intention behind the show. Several of the works address real issues: contamination in mining regions, the privatisation of supply and the long walks to collect water that still occupy many women in the world. These are matters that deserve attention, and the museum has done well to give them a platform. It is simply unfortunate that the sheer quantity of earnest material tends to dull its force. Seriousness, when it never pauses, can sound a little like noise.

The gallery layout does not help. Visitors are guided through a continuous, winding route and, since the walls are painted a consistent blue, the effect is of being slowly submerged. The lighting, which is dim throughout, makes some of the smaller pieces almost impossible to read. I saw a family abandon the fourth room after a child, reasonably enough, asked whether there was a way to the cafe. That, one suspects, was the most honest reaction of the afternoon.

Nor is the show without moments of real wonder. In the final room, a single large drop of water falls, every ninety seconds, onto a metal plate, producing a note that echoes through the empty space. The piece, by a young Colombian sculptor whose name the museum has placed in the smallest type available, is spare, patient and, remarkably, funny, since a number of visitors began to wait for the drop with the anxiety of people watching a penalty shoot-out.

I would advise visitors to go, but to go selectively. Skip the wall texts, linger over the quiet works and leave before fatigue sets in. The Weight of Water is an ambitious show with excellent ingredients, undermined by an unwillingness to trust them. It reminds one of a good soup to which a nervous cook has kept adding salt. The result is not inedible, merely so earnest that one longs, just for a moment, for a glass of plain water.

title: Let Students Fail Once
topic: Higher education and the fear of failure
paragraphs: A first-year student at a Chilean university recently told our reporter that she had not slept properly in six weeks. She was not studying more than before. She was, as she put it, 'afraid of ruining my record', a record that would be examined, she believed, by every future employer. Her anxiety is not a personal quirk. It is the predictable product of a system that treats a single failed course as a permanent stain, and it is time to ask whether that system serves anyone.

The logic of the stain is easy to understand. In a labour market that looks for quick signals, grades are convenient, and institutions have responded by making them heavier. A transcript is now less a record of learning than a ledger of risk, and a prudent student, quite rationally, avoids any course in which she might do badly. The perverse result is that the most capable young people are tempted to choose easy subjects and to avoid the demanding ones that would teach them most.

We should not pretend that failure is pleasant, and nobody in this editorial's circle romanticises it. A failed examination costs money, delays a degree and, for families who have sacrificed to pay the fees, can feel like a small disaster. Nor do we suggest that standards should be lowered. A degree that anyone can obtain would be worthless to everyone, and the graduates who worked hardest would be the first to suffer. The question is not whether to expect excellence but how to teach it.

Research on learning, much of it unglamorous, suggests that mistakes made in a low-risk environment are among the most effective teachers. A student who tries to solve a difficult problem, fails and then sees the correct method tends to remember it far longer than one who has been shown the answer first. Failure, in other words, is not the opposite of learning but frequently its mechanism. A system that punishes it severely teaches students, above all, to hide it.

There are practical ways to reduce the cost of failing. Universities could allow every student to repeat one course in the degree without penalty, removing the original grade from the transcript. Courses could also be designed with low-stakes assignments early on, so that errors occur when they matter least. Some institutions elsewhere have adopted pass-fail grading for first-year subjects, and report no collapse in standards and, notably, fewer students dropping out.

Sceptics will say that such reforms invite carelessness, since a student with a safety net may stop trying. The danger is real but, in our view, overstated. A single repeated course is not a licence to idle; it is the difference between a mistake and a catastrophe. The student who uses the opportunity well will profit from it, and the one who does not will, in any case, be caught by the same examinations that have always protected the value of the degree.

Universities like to speak of resilience, and they hold seminars about it, usually in the same weeks in which they publish ranking tables that reward perfect records. It is time to align what is said with what is done. If we truly want graduates who can take risks, think originally and recover from setbacks, we must first allow them to have one. Let students fail once, and let them discover that the world, contrary to what the transcript implies, continues.
